newsitem.title: USA: Dlr closes up in U.S., buoyant above 110 yen.
newsitem.headline: Dlr closes up in U.S., buoyant above 110 yen.

text.p: The dollar closed above 110 yen for the first time in nearly two months fanned higher by remarks from Eisuke Sakakibara and speculation U.S./Japanese interest rate differentials will continue to favor the dollar.
Sakakibara, director general the Ministry's International Finance Bureau told reporters that Japan has no specific target for the dollar/yen rate.

"It's a continuation of the prospects of no Japanese rate hike in the near future, Sakakibara's comment and break of the psychological 110 yen level," said Bill Marr, foreign exchange manager at Credit Commercial de France.
"Those three things are what's getting us through," he said.
The dollar closed at 110.35/40 yen -- its highest U.S. close since July 12 -- up from 110.06/13 at the open.
After rising to a fresh eight-week high at 1.5155 marks in Europe, the dollar closed at 1.5110/15 marks, up from 1.5095/00 at the open.

Sakakibara -- "dubbed Mr. Yen" by the market -- is the architect of Japan's 1995 offshore investment deregulation package, which many consider the catalyst for the dollar's rise from its historic low under 80 yen last year.
He seemed to refute comments reported from another economic official who suggested Japan preferred a 105-to-110 yen range for the dollar.
His comments dovetailed with those of U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who reiterated his support for a strong dollar to reporters late Wednesday.

The yen's slide against the dollar Wednesday was also fueled by ongoing speculation Japan's weak economy and recent bankruptcies in Japan's financial community have killed any chance of higher Japanese interest rates soon.
"Interest rate differentials are in favor of the dollar and the differentials are going to increase," said Tom Sharpe, assistant mananger of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank.
U.S. inflation data later in the week may recieve extra scrutiny following Federal Reserve Governor Janet Yellen's comment Tuesday that the U.S. economy was in an "inflationary danger zone".
"There is no question people are probably looking to take profits ahead of inflation figures in the U.S.," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole.
Wall Street economists polled by Reuters expect August producer prices to rise 0.1 percent on Thursday and August consumer prices to rise 0.2 percent on Friday.

But even before Yellen's remarks, the market was discounting a Fed credit tightening after several weeks of strong economic data, particularly Friday's drop in the August unemployment rate to 5.1 percent from 5.4 percent.
Traders have been buying dollar's in expectation that the Fed would boost short-term interest rates when its policy makers meet on September 24.
But the Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday, showed the economy to be growing moderately with no clear sign of higher inflation.
"The Beige Book was a little bit of a disappointment to those who think we're going to get a hike, but I still think we're going to get a hike soon," said Sharpe.
In other trade, the dollar rose to 1.2352/62 Swiss from 1.2325/35 at the open and it fell to Canadian $1.3711/16 from C$1.3715/20.
The pound was barely changed at $1.5547/54 and the Australian dollar fell to $0.7986/91 from $0.8005/10.
-- Alden Bentley 212 859 1667
